Iterates over the bindings that run `action`, in the order they were added.

Bindings disabled by a later [`NoAction`](crate::NoAction) or [`Unbind`](crate::Unbind) are
left out. This ignores key contexts, so a binding is included even when it can't fire in the
current focus. To find the bindings that apply now, use
[`Window::bindings_for_action`](crate::Window::bindings_for_action). For a shortcut label,
use the last binding, which was added most recently.

Returns a list of bindings that match the given input, and a boolean indicating whether or
not more bindings might match if the input was longer. Bindings are returned in precedence
order (higher precedence first, reverse of the order they were added to the keymap).

Precedence is defined by the depth in the tree (matches on the Editor take precedence over
matches on the Pane, then the Workspace, etc.). Bindings with no context are treated as the
same as the deepest context.

In the case of multiple bindings at the same depth, the ones added to the keymap later take
precedence. User bindings are added after built-in bindings so that they take precedence.

If a user has disabled a binding with `"x": null` it will not be returned. Disabled bindings
are evaluated with the same precedence rules so you can disable a rule in a given context
only.

Returns a list of bindings that match the given input, and a boolean indicating whether or
not more bindings might match if the input was longer. Bindings are returned in precedence

Precedence is defined by the depth in the tree (matches on the Editor take precedence over
matches on the Pane, then the Workspace, etc.). Bindings with no context are treated as the
same as the deepest context.

d.1:3:
Returns the bindings that match `input` in `context_stack`, and whether a longer input
could still match a binding.

The first value holds the matching bindings, highest precedence first. The second value is
`true` when some binding needs more keystrokes than `input`, so the caller should wait for
the next keystroke.

Precedence works as follows:

- **Depth.** A binding's depth is the deepest point in `context_stack` where its predicate
  matches. A binding in a deeper context wins over one in a shallower context. A binding
  without a context is as deep as the stack, so it is at least as deep as any
  context-specific binding. At equal depth, the order rule below decides.
- **Order.** At the same depth, the binding added later wins.
- **`NoAction`.** A winning [`NoAction`](crate::NoAction) removes the lower-precedence
  bindings for the same keystrokes, unless they come from a stronger source. See
  [`KeyBindingMetaIndex`](crate::KeyBindingMetaIndex).
- **`Unbind`.** A winning [`Unbind`](crate::Unbind) removes the lower-precedence binding for
  the same keystrokes that runs the action it names, whatever that binding's context.

Several bindings can be returned, because a match that isn't suppressed stays in the list.

# Examples

```standalone_crate
use gpui::{Action, KeyBinding, KeyContext, Keymap, Keystroke, actions};

actions!(input_docs, [Save, Format]);

let keymap = Keymap::new(vec![
    KeyBinding::new("cmd-s", Format, Some("Workspace")),
    KeyBinding::new("cmd-s", Save, Some("Editor")),
]);

// The `Editor` binding is at depth 2 and the `Workspace` binding at depth 1.
let (bindings, _) = keymap.bindings_for_input(
    &[Keystroke::parse("cmd-s").unwrap()],
    &[
        KeyContext::parse("Workspace").unwrap(),
        KeyContext::parse("Editor").unwrap(),
    ],
);
assert_eq!(bindings[0].action().name(), "input_docs::Save");
```

d.1:3:
Parses a keystroke from text such as `cmd-s`, `ctrl-shift-tab` or `cmd--`.

The syntax is zero or more modifiers, then a key, separated by `-`:

- **Modifiers** are `ctrl`, `alt`, `shift`, `fn`, `secondary`, `cmd`, `super` and `win`.
  They can come in any order and any case. `cmd`, `super` and `win` all set
  [`Modifiers::platform`]. `secondary` sets `cmd` on macOS and `ctrl` on other platforms,
  which is what [`Modifiers::secondary`] reports.
- **The key** is the last part. Any other part must be a modifier. Key names are
  case-insensitive and stored in lowercase, so `Tab` and `tab` are the same key. Other
  text is accepted as a key without checking, but the names that platforms produce are
  `space`, `tab`, `enter`, `backspace`, `escape`, `delete`, `insert`, `home`, `end`,
  `pageup`, `pagedown`, `up`, `down`, `left`, `right` and function keys such as `f1`.
- **A single uppercase letter** sets `shift` and uses the lowercase letter as the key, so
  `S` is `shift-s`.
- **A key of `-`** is written as an extra dash, so `cmd--` is `cmd` and `-`.
- **A modifier with no key** becomes the key. The first of `shift`, `ctrl`, `alt`, `cmd` and
  `fn` that is present is used, in that order. Its key is named `shift`, `control`, `alt`,
  `platform` or `function`, and that modifier is cleared. So `ctrl` alone is the key
  `control` with no modifiers set.
- **`key->key_char`** sets `key_char` to the text after `->`, for example `alt-s->ß`.
  [`Keystroke::should_match`] ignores it when matching a binding.

Returns [`InvalidKeystrokeError`] if a part before the key isn't a modifier, as in
`ctrl-a-b`, or if `->` isn't followed by a key character.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::Keystroke;
let save = Keystroke::parse("secondary-s").unwrap();
assert!(save.modifiers.secondary());
assert_eq!(save.key, "s");

let shifted = Keystroke::parse("S").unwrap();
assert!(shifted.modifiers.shift);
assert_eq!(shifted.key, "s");

assert!(Keystroke::parse("ctrl-a-b").is_err());
```

See [keyboard input](crate::_documentation::guides::keyboard) for how bindings use these.

When matching a key we cannot know whether the user intended to type
the key_char or the key itself. On some non-US keyboards keys we use in our
bindings are behind option (for example `$` is typed `alt-ç` on a Czech keyboard),
and on some keyboards the IME handler converts a sequence of keys into a
specific character (for example `"` is typed as `" space` on a brazilian keyboard).

This method assumes that `self` was typed and `target' is in the keymap, and checks
both possibilities for self against the target.

d.1:3:
Returns whether this keystroke, as typed, matches a keystroke in a keymap.

`self` is the keystroke the user typed and `target` is the one from the binding. Matching
first compares modifiers and key. It also accepts a `target` whose key is this keystroke's
`key_char`, when the target's modifiers are exactly this keystroke's `ctrl` and `cmd` (on
Windows, when the target has no modifiers). That covers layouts where a binding
key sits behind option, such as `$` on a Czech keyboard typed as `alt-ç`, and input methods
that turn a sequence of keys into one character.

Returns this keystroke with `key_char` set to the text it would type.

Simulated keystrokes use this so that they type text as a real key press does. It only
applies when `key_char` is `None` and none of `cmd`, `ctrl`, `fn` or `alt` is held. `space`,

character, uppercased when `shift` is held.
